title: Everyday economics: costs, incentives, and trade-offs
description: Thirty questions on the economics of everyday choices. You'll practice **opportunity cost**, **sunk costs**, **marginal cost**, **fixed and variable costs**, incentives that backfire, scarcity and trade-offs, **diminishing returns**, and the hidden price of *free*. Expect concept questions (single choice), spot-every-example scenarios (multiple choice), and quick calculations (numeric input). Each explanation shows why the tempting wrong answer is wrong, and every question links to Wikipedia so you can check it and read more.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: What does *opportunity cost* mean?

options.text: The value of the best single alternative you give up when you make a choice
The total value of every option you didn't choose, added together
The amount of cash you actually pay for something
A cost you've already paid and can't get back

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the **best single alternative** you give up. It isn't the sum of every option you skipped, and it isn't the cash you spend. If studying tonight means giving up an $80 shift or a $30 evening out, the opportunity cost is $80, because you could only have done one of them. It also covers implicit costs, like the rent a firm could earn from a building it already owns.

questions.title: You have one free evening. You could work an $80 extra shift, go to a $50 concert, or relax at home (worth about $30 to you). You pick the concert. What's the *opportunity cost*?

options.text: $80, the value of the best alternative you gave up (the shift)
$110, the shift and the relaxing added together
$50, the price of the concert ticket
$0, because you chose what you wanted

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost counts only the most valuable thing you gave up: the $80 shift. You couldn't have done both the shift and the relaxing, so adding them up to $110 overcounts. The $50 ticket is an *explicit* cost, the money you pay, which is a separate thing. And the answer is never $0, because a free evening can only be used once.

questions.title: Which of these involve a real *opportunity cost*?

options.text: Working an extra paid shift on your only free Saturday instead of resting
Spending $2,000 of savings on a holiday instead of investing it
A bakery running its shop in a building it owns instead of renting the building out
The $400 you paid for last year's gym membership and never used
Taking the only option available when there's truly no alternative

questions.explanation: There's an opportunity cost whenever your time, your money, or even a building could have gone to some other valuable use. The bakery's lost rent is an **implicit** cost: accountants usually leave it out, but economists count it. Last year's gym fee is a sunk cost. It's already gone, so it isn't an alternative you can still choose. And if you have no alternative at all, there's nothing to give up, so the opportunity cost is zero.

questions.title: An outdoor concert is *free* to enter, but going means skipping a 4-hour shift that pays $15/hour and spending $12 on gas. What's the total economic cost of going, in dollars? (Enter a number.)
questions.explanation: Economic cost is what you pay plus what you give up. Here that's $12 for gas plus the $60 you'd have earned (4 × $15), so **$72**. The $0 ticket price hides most of the cost, which is the wages you don't earn that evening.

questions.title: You bought a $15 movie ticket in advance. By showtime you feel sick and would rather stay home. Which cost is *sunk*?

options.text: The $15 you already paid, which is gone whether you go or not
The enjoyment you'd get from the film
Medicine you might buy if you stay home
The bus fare to the cinema, which you haven't paid yet

questions.explanation: A **sunk cost** is money, time, or effort you've already spent and can't get back, whatever you do next. The $15 is gone either way, so leave it out of the decision. What matters now is how you feel and what each choice will cost and give you from here. The bus fare isn't sunk, because staying home still saves it.

questions.title: What is the *sunk cost fallacy*?

options.text: Sticking with something because of what you've already spent, instead of judging its future costs and benefits
Refusing to spend money on big, long-term projects
Always picking the cheapest option right now
Ignoring the future when making a decision

questions.explanation: Good decisions look only at future costs and benefits, because you can't change the past. The fallacy is thinking 'I've put in too much to stop now' and throwing good money after bad. It's also called the **Concorde fallacy**, after the supersonic airliner that kept getting funded long after it made economic sense, because so much had already been spent on it.

questions.title: Fill in the blank: keeping a failing plan going only because of the time or money you've already put in is the '___ ___ fallacy.' (Give the two words before *fallacy*.)
questions.explanation: The answer is **sunk cost**. The mistake is treating money you can't recover as a reason to keep going, when the decision should depend only on what happens next. You'll spot it in daily life: finishing a meal you don't like because you paid for it, or staying in a course you hate because of the fees.

questions.title: What is *marginal cost*?

options.text: The extra cost of producing one more unit
The total cost of everything produced so far
The average cost per unit across the whole batch
The profit earned on the last unit sold

questions.explanation: Marginal cost is how much total cost goes up when you make one more unit. **Total cost** is the running sum, and **average cost** is total cost divided by quantity. Use marginal cost when you ask 'should I make, buy, or do one more?', because the next unit's cost is the only one you can still change.

questions.title: A gym charges a flat $40/month for unlimited visits, with no per-visit fee. Ignoring travel, what's the marginal cost of one more visit this month, in dollars? (Enter a number.)
questions.explanation: The $40 is a **fixed** cost. You pay it whether you go zero times or thirty, so one more visit adds nothing: the marginal cost is **$0**. People often divide $40 by their number of visits to get a 'cost per visit', but that's the *average* cost. Once the membership is paid, any visit you'd enjoy even a little is worth making.

questions.title: A bakery spends $120 in total to bake 50 loaves and $122 to bake 51. What's the marginal cost of the 51st loaf, in dollars? (Enter a number.)
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the change in total cost: $122 − $120 = **$2**. The average cost so far is higher: $120 ÷ 50 = $2.40. Since the 51st loaf costs less than the average, baking it pulls the average down. That's why marginal and average cost are different numbers, and why decisions should use the marginal one.

questions.title: A workshop can make 100 chairs for $4,000 in total, or 120 chairs for $4,500. Over that range, what's the marginal cost per extra chair, in dollars? (Enter a number.)
questions.explanation: When output grows by more than one unit, divide the change in total cost by the change in quantity: ($4,500 − $4,000) ÷ (120 − 100) = $500 ÷ 20 = **$25** per chair. Compare that number with what each extra chair brings in to decide whether the bigger run is worth it.

questions.title: Economists say good decisions are made 'at the margin.' What does that mean?

options.text: Comparing the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost, and ignoring sunk costs
Always picking the option with the lowest total cost
Only acting when something is free
Dividing total cost by quantity and comparing the averages

questions.explanation: Thinking at the margin means asking about the *next* unit. Is one more hour of study, one more coffee, or one more item produced worth what it adds in cost? Keep going while the extra benefit is bigger than the extra cost, and stop when it isn't. Sunk costs drop out on their own, because the next unit doesn't change them.

questions.title: Which is the best example of a *fixed cost* for a small café?

options.text: The monthly rent on the café space
The coffee beans used for each cup
The milk poured into each latte
Hourly pay for extra weekend staff

questions.explanation: A **fixed cost** stays the same in the short run, however much you sell. The café pays the same rent whether it sells 1 cup or 1,000. Beans, milk, and extra staff hours all grow as it serves more, so they're *variable* costs. Fixed costs are why a quiet day is still expensive.

questions.title: For the same café, which of these are *variable costs* that rise as it serves more cups?

options.text: Coffee beans
Milk
Disposable cups and lids
The monthly rent
A flat annual insurance premium paid up front

questions.explanation: **Variable costs** go up and down with output: every extra cup needs more beans, more milk, and another cup and lid. Rent and a flat insurance premium stay the same however busy the café is, so they're **fixed costs**. Add the two together and you get total cost. Knowing the split tells you how profit changes as sales grow.

questions.title: Fill in the blank: in the short run, a firm's **total cost** equals its fixed costs plus its ___ costs.
questions.explanation: Total cost = fixed costs + **variable** costs. As output grows, the fixed part stays flat and the variable part rises. So the average cost per unit usually falls at first, because the fixed cost is spread over more units. It rises again once variable costs start climbing steeply.

questions.title: A government pays a bounty for every dead cobra, hoping to reduce the number of cobras. Instead, people start *breeding* cobras to collect the money, and the population grows. What's an incentive that backfires like this called?

options.text: A perverse incentive (the 'cobra effect')
A sunk cost
A fixed cost
An opportunity cost

questions.explanation: A **perverse incentive** leads to the opposite of what its designers wanted, because people respond to the reward as written instead of its purpose. Economist Horst Siebert coined the name *cobra effect*. Historians dispute whether the cobra story really happened. A well-documented case is the 1902 rat-tail bounty in Hanoi under French colonial rule: rat catchers bred rats and released tailless ones so the bounties would keep coming. People optimize for exactly what you reward, so design incentives carefully.

questions.title: In economics, what is an *incentive*?

options.text: Something that motivates behavior by changing the costs or benefits people face
A tax the government collects each year
A cost that's already been spent
The total amount a firm produces

questions.explanation: An incentive is any reward or penalty that changes the costs and benefits of an action and so nudges behavior. Discounts, fines, bonuses, and subsidies are all incentives. People respond to incentives, often in ways the designer didn't expect, and that's where unintended consequences come from.

questions.title: Which of these are examples of *incentives with unintended consequences*?

options.text: Paying programmers per line of code, which rewards bloated, padded code
A rat-tail bounty that leads people to farm rats for their tails
Basing a teacher's bonus only on test scores, which leads to teaching to the test
A per-unit sales tax that raises the price buyers pay
A discount that increases sales of a product, as planned

questions.explanation: These incentives backfire because people chase the letter of the reward: more code instead of better software, more rats instead of fewer, and test prep instead of learning. This is close to **Goodhart's law**: 'when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.' A sales tax raising prices and a discount boosting sales are the intended effects, so they don't count.

questions.title: In economics, what does *scarcity* mean?

options.text: Resources are limited but wants are practically unlimited, so we have to choose
A temporary shortage caused by a delivery delay
Something being rare and therefore expensive, like a diamond
Running out of money at the end of the month

questions.explanation: Scarcity is the basic condition economics studies. Time, money, and resources are limited, while wants aren't, so you can't have everything and have to choose. It's broader than a one-off shortage or a single rare item. Scarcity is what creates trade-offs and opportunity costs in the first place.

questions.title: A country with a fixed budget can build more hospitals or more tanks, but not the maximum of both. What's this classic example of a *trade-off* called?

options.text: The guns versus butter model
The sunk cost fallacy
The cobra effect
Diminishing marginal utility

questions.explanation: The **guns versus butter** model is the textbook picture of a trade-off. When resources are fully used, making more 'guns' (military goods) means making less 'butter' (civilian goods). Each extra tank costs the hospitals and schools that weren't built. Your own budget works the same way: a dollar or an hour spent here can't be spent there.

questions.title: How are a *trade-off* and an *opportunity cost* related?

options.text: A trade-off is giving up one thing to get another; the opportunity cost is the value of the best thing given up
They're the same thing with two names
Trade-offs involve only money; opportunity cost involves only time
Opportunity cost applies to firms; trade-offs apply only to individuals

questions.explanation: A **trade-off** is the fact that, because of scarcity, getting more of one thing means accepting less of another. The **opportunity cost** puts a value on that sacrifice: it's the worth of the best alternative you gave up. Every choice involves a trade-off, and opportunity cost is how economists put a price on it.

questions.title: What point does the saying 'there's no such thing as a free lunch' (TANSTAAFL) make?

options.text: Things that look free still cost something, paid by someone else or in alternatives you give up
Restaurants should never give food away
Lunch is the most important purchase of the day
Anything offered for free is a scam

questions.explanation: The saying comes from 19th-century American saloons that gave a 'free' lunch to anyone who bought a drink. The food was salty, so people bought more beer, and the beer paid for the lunch. Economist Milton Friedman made the phrase popular. Because resources are scarce, a benefit to one person is almost always paid for somewhere: in money, in someone else's cost, or in the alternatives you give up. Free offers usually aren't scams. The cost is just hidden or moved to someone else.

questions.title: A phone app costs nothing to download or use. What's its most likely *hidden cost*?

options.text: Your time, attention, and personal data, which the app makes money from, often through ads
There's no cost of any kind
Only the electricity used to charge your phone
A secret monthly fee the app charges automatically

questions.explanation: When you don't pay with money, you usually pay with attention and data. Hence the saying 'if you're not paying for the product, you *are* the product.' Your time has an opportunity cost too, since you could spend those hours on something else you value. The app has no secret fee, but its price isn't in dollars.

questions.title: A supermarket sells milk below its own cost to bring shoppers in, expecting them to fill their baskets with profitable items too. What's this pricing tactic called?

options.text: A loss leader
A sunk cost
A fixed cost
A perverse incentive

questions.explanation: A **loss leader** is priced below cost on purpose. It brings in customers who then buy enough higher-margin goods to make the visit profitable for the store. Staples like milk and bananas are common loss leaders, and stores often put them at the back so you walk past other products to reach them. A striking bargain is usually part of the seller's larger plan.

questions.title: What does the *law of diminishing returns* say?

options.text: If you keep adding one input while the others stay fixed, the extra output from each added unit eventually falls
Output falls as soon as you add any input
The more you produce, the cheaper each unit gets, forever
Each extra unit you buy is more enjoyable than the last

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns is about *production*. Add more of one input while everything else stays fixed, like more cooks in one small kitchen, and total output still rises. But each new cook adds less than the one before, because they get in each other's way. It's the extra output per added unit that shrinks, not necessarily the total.

questions.title: On a fixed plot of land, 1 worker harvests 10 baskets, 2 workers harvest 18 in total, and 3 workers harvest 24 in total. What's the *marginal product* of the 3rd worker, in extra baskets? (Enter a number.)
questions.explanation: Marginal product is the output the next worker adds: 24 − 18 = **6** baskets. The 1st worker adds 10, the 2nd adds 8, and the 3rd adds 6. Total output keeps growing, but in smaller steps on the same plot. That shrinking sequence is diminishing returns.

questions.title: When you're hungry, the first slice of pizza is delicious, the fourth is just okay, and the sixth feels like a chore. What's this called?

options.text: Diminishing marginal utility
The sunk cost fallacy
A fixed cost
A perverse incentive

questions.explanation: **Diminishing marginal utility** is the consumer's version of diminishing returns: each extra unit you consume adds less satisfaction than the one before. It's why you stop buying once the next slice is worth less to you than its price. Diminishing *returns* is about adding inputs to production, and diminishing marginal *utility* is about consuming more.

questions.title: Which of these are everyday examples of *diminishing returns or diminishing marginal utility*?

options.text: Your 3rd coffee of the day gives much less of a boost than the 1st
A 5th straight hour of cramming adds far fewer points than the 1st hour did
A 6th cook in a tiny kitchen barely increases the number of meals served
Doubling a recipe doubles every ingredient you need
Monthly rent that stays the same however much you produce

questions.explanation: In the three correct examples, each extra unit brings a smaller extra gain: the 3rd coffee, the 5th hour of study, the 6th cook. Doubling a recipe is simple **proportional** scaling (constant returns), and rent that doesn't change is a **fixed cost**. Neither shows a shrinking gain.

questions.title: A coffee shop offers unlimited coffee for $40/month. Otherwise you'd buy your usual 25 coffees a month at $2 each, which is $50. What percentage do you save each month by subscribing? (Enter the number only, e.g. 20 for 20%.)
questions.explanation: Buying cups one at a time costs 25 × $2 = $50. The subscription costs $40, so you save $10, and $10 ÷ $50 = **20%**. There's a catch: once you've paid the $40, one more cup costs you nothing, which can tempt you to drink coffee you don't really want. You only save money if your normal drinking makes the flat fee cheaper than paying per cup.

questions.title: Which question best sums up *thinking like an economist* about an everyday choice?

options.text: What do I give up by choosing this, and is the extra benefit worth the extra cost?
How much have I already spent on this?
What's the grand total cost of everything, added up?
What would other people think of my choice?

questions.explanation: Economic thinking looks forward and at the margin. It asks what the **opportunity cost** is, meaning the best alternative you give up, and whether the extra benefit of the next step beats its extra cost. It ignores sunk costs and doesn't fixate on grand totals. With those two habits, scarcity, trade-offs, marginal cost, and sunk cost all fit together as one way of looking at choices.
